sections.overview: Since an IUCN specialist-group review in 2025, Giraffa camelopardalis is treated as the Northern Giraffe, one of four recognized giraffe species. The older one-species classification has therefore been superseded in this specialist framework.
sections.identification: It is the world’s tallest living land mammal, with a long neck and legs and a coat patterned in irregular patches.
sections.habitat: Northern giraffes persist in scattered populations across parts of northern and central Africa, including the Sahel and East-Central Africa.
sections.diet: Giraffes browse leaves and shoots, especially from trees such as acacias; the neck and prehensile tongue help them reach foliage.
sections.behavior: They move between feeding and resting sites and may form loose, changing groups rather than fixed herds.
sections.reproduction: Giraffes give birth to a single calf after a long gestation; this general giraffe pattern is not a Northern-giraffe-specific measure.
sections.ecology: The 2025 taxonomic change separates Northern giraffes from reticulated, Masai and southern giraffes, whose ranges and conservation needs differ. The Spanish report likewise contrasts their ranges and conservation needs.
sections.conservation: The Giraffe Conservation Foundation estimated 7,037 Northern giraffes in its 2025 report; this is a compiled estimate, not a new IUCN Red List assessment.
